nodes.label: UmbraDB
nodes.rationale: A local, persistent, single-writer datastore for Midnight blockchain clients. TypeScript, ESM-only, Node >= 24. Deliberately a library over PostgreSQL with no ORM: the caller supplies the database, UmbraDB owns a schema inside it.

nodes.label: Full PostgreSQL to SQLite replacement question
nodes.rationale: Scope fixed by the repo owner: SQLite becomes THE engine and src/postgres/ is eventually deleted. Explicitly not a dual-backend study, because designing an abstraction seam would be wasted effort unless a lane proves full replacement impossible without one. Everything is in scope including the multi-hundred-GB chain archive at ~1 GB/hour ingest.
nodes.norm_label: full postgresql to sqlite replacement question

nodes.label: TemporalKV primitive
nodes.rationale: Versioned KV with point-in-time reads; the surface that carries laws T3 and T5.

nodes.label: CheckpointStore primitive
nodes.rationale: Content-addressed, deduplicated, chunked snapshot storage with GC; carries C1 (save-side chunk projection as a join-semilattice) and C2a (GC reachability safety).

nodes.label: Watermarks primitive
nodes.rationale: Unversioned sync-progress cursors, deliberately last-write-wins (law W1) rather than versioned, because a cursor has no meaningful history.

nodes.label: Transaction/Lease primitive
nodes.rationale: Real Postgres transactions plus connection-pinned advisory locks; enforces L1 lease mutual exclusion at runtime rather than by proof.

nodes.label: TransactionHistory primitive
nodes.rationale: Per-wallet tx history, GIN-indexed on an identifiers array so containment queries over identifiers stay cheap.

nodes.label: WalletStateEnvelope capability
nodes.rationale: Built from CheckpointStore: a whole wallet-sync snapshot in one save() call.

nodes.label: saveAndAdvance co-transactional cursor primitive
nodes.rationale: CheckpointStore plus Watermarks in one transaction, so a snapshot and its cursor advance are both durable at one commit or neither — the G5 co-transactionality guarantee.

nodes.label: Chain archive
nodes.rationale: chain_blobs, blocks, transactions, bridge_observations at multi-hundred-GB scale with ~1 GB/hour ingest via chain-archive-sync/. Explicitly in scope rather than carved out, so any SQLite verdict must survive archive-scale write pressure.

nodes.label: Formal cut-line {T3, T5, W1, C1}
nodes.rationale: Mechanized in Lean 4 under Formal/Lean/ and CI-gated: lean.yml rejects any sorry/admit/axiom/unsafe, builds, then independently leancheckers the tree. Cut here rather than wider because the Lean layer models only an abstract store.

nodes.label: T3 — temporal projection / observational equivalence
nodes.rationale: Point-in-time reads within retention are observationally equivalent to reading the store as of that instant. Lean-mechanized.

nodes.label: T5 — temporal coherence (interval non-overlap + gap-freedom)
nodes.rationale: Enforced at runtime not by application code but by a btree_gist EXCLUDE constraint over a generated tstzrange validity column — the constraint IS the enforcement.

nodes.label: C2a — GC reachability-safety
nodes.rationale: MECHANISM SPECIFIED, not proved: enforced at runtime by a same-transaction reachability scan and tested by P8, rather than mechanized in Lean.

nodes.label: L1 — lease mutual exclusion
nodes.rationale: MECHANISM SPECIFIED, not proved: enforced by a session-scoped advisory lock and tested by P10. Deliberately unconditional (no TTL, no self-expiry, no stealing) because a TTL design cannot guarantee mutual exclusion for arbitrary caller code without fencing tokens.

nodes.label: Trusted unmechanized abstract-to-concrete refinement bridge
nodes.rationale: The Lean layer models an abstract store; the abstract to PostgreSQL/TypeScript refinement is explicitly a trusted, unmechanized bridge (the AWS TLA+ stance), bridged empirically by the P1-P10 conformance suite. The open question is what that trusted bridge becomes when the concrete store changes engine.

nodes.label: P1–P10 conformance suite
nodes.rationale: The empirical bridge that stands in for a mechanized refinement proof; P8 tests C2a, P10 tests L1.

nodes.label: G1 — frozen public API surface
nodes.rationale: A single barrel src/index.ts, strict exports map, no deep imports. DEFAULT_SCHEMA and schema-configurability are part of that surface.

nodes.label: G2 — SemVer + CHANGELOG
nodes.rationale: No incompatible change to the exported surface or the error code set in a minor/patch.

nodes.label: G3 — frozen error catalog
nodes.rationale: 25 codes with a machine-readable retryable field; frozen retryable set {CONNECTION_ERROR, TRANSACTION_FAULT, LEASE_TIMEOUT, MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT}. Drift-tested against the exported surface. STABILITY.md forbids removing, renaming, or repurposing a code within 1.x.

nodes.label: G4 — eight written release contracts
nodes.rationale: docs/CONTRACT.md: durability, forward-only migration, cancellation, save-retry, lease limitation, backup/restore, threat-model pointer, format headroom.

nodes.label: btree_gist EXCLUDE constraint on validity
nodes.rationale: EXCLUDE USING gist (ns WITH =, scope WITH =, key WITH =, validity WITH &&) over a GENERATED ALWAYS AS STORED tstzrange column. Chosen because the constraint IS how T5 non-overlap is enforced at runtime — the database, not application code, is the enforcement point.

nodes.label: kv_current_history_trigger plpgsql trigger
nodes.rationale: BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW; uses txid_current() to reject a second write to the same key in the same transaction (custom SQLSTATE UB001) and writes the history row. Put in the database so the invariant cannot be bypassed by any caller path.

nodes.label: clock_timestamp() temporal boundaries
nodes.rationale: clock_timestamp() + date_trunc('milliseconds', ...) is used deliberately instead of now(), because now() is transaction-scoped and would collapse distinct temporal boundaries inside one transaction.

nodes.label: pg_advisory_lock session-scoped lease
nodes.rationale: pg_advisory_lock / pg_try_advisory_lock / pg_advisory_xact_lock, session-scoped and pinned to a reserved connection via sql.reserve(). Its decisive property is server-side release on holder death with no heartbeat and no stale-takeover rule.

nodes.label: GIN index with <@ containment on text[]
nodes.norm_label: gin index with <@ containment on text[]

nodes.label: PARTITION BY RANGE on chain-archive tables
nodes.rationale: PARTITION BY RANGE (height) / (block_height) with a _default partition and partition-compatible unique indexes — the mechanism that keeps multi-hundred-GB archive tables manageable.
nodes.norm_label: partition by range on chain-archive tables

nodes.label: CREATE SCHEMA + search_path isolation
nodes.rationale: How UmbraDB owns a schema inside a caller-supplied database and makes the schema name configurable — part of the frozen G1 surface via DEFAULT_SCHEMA.

nodes.label: Query.prototype.cancel() protocol-level cancellation
nodes.rationale: Real protocol-level query cancellation sent on a second connection; the substrate for the published G4 cancellation contract.

nodes.label: postgres.js driver
nodes.rationale: Chosen with no ORM so the caller supplies the database and query text stays literal SQL; its tagged-template shape and OID-driven row decoding become the compatibility target for any SQLite shim.

nodes.label: node:sqlite built into Node v24.18.0
nodes.rationale: Ground truth established before dispatch: node:sqlite is built in and working, sqlite_version() 3.53.1, so real SQLite experiments run with zero installation. Measured behavior beats cited behavior.

nodes.label: Trap: WSL/Windows path trap
nodes.rationale: Tools run on Windows while the repo lives in WSL; a bare /root/... path resolves on the Windows drive and silently creates or reads phantom files. Always use the \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-26.04\root\... UNC prefix.

nodes.label: Trap: beware the confident negative
nodes.rationale: A prior round recorded 'lever spent — measured no gain' and had to retract it because the measurement was masked by a much larger cost elsewhere. Any negative result must state what would have had to be true for the measurement to be meaningful.

nodes.label: Trap: a green gate certifies depth, never breadth
nodes.rationale: 0 sorry in Lean proves that what is stated is proved; it cannot detect a missing or too-weak law. CI green is not coverage.
nodes.norm_label: trap: a green gate certifies depth, never breadth

nodes.label: Trap: do not run npm install in the worktree
nodes.rationale: Not needed (node:sqlite is built in), slow, and npm installs in this project's neighbourhood have previously destroyed an adjacent checkout's node_modules through a symlink.
nodes.norm_label: trap: do not run npm install in the worktree

nodes.label: Per-key sidecar SQLite lock file lease
nodes.rationale: CHOSEN lease design. A tiny sidecar DB per lease key held open under BEGIN IMMEDIATE. Chosen because it reproduces pg_advisory_lock's decisive property — kernel releases the fcntl lock on SIGKILL, successor acquired in 0 ms, no heartbeat and no takeover rule — with zero dependencies, per-key granularity, and mutual exclusion both cross-process and between two connections in one process. It also strengthens L1: the lock moves from the connection's failure domain to the process's, so the 'mutual exclusion may have lapsed' hazard becomes essentially unreachable and CONTRACT.md §5 can be upgraded from 'a second writer process is unsupported' to 'refused'.
nodes.norm_label: per-key sidecar sqlite lock file lease

nodes.label: BEGIN IMMEDIATE
nodes.rationale: Chosen over DEFERRED for withTransaction, saveAndAdvance and prune. DEFERRED takes no write lock at BEGIN, so the first write attempts an upgrade that yields SQLITE_BUSY or SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT (517) mid-callback — and 517 is not retried by the busy handler and does not auto-rollback. IMMEDIATE converts that unavoidable mid-callback failure into a bounded wait at BEGIN, where the callback has not yet run and a retry is free.

nodes.label: PRAGMA busy_timeout
nodes.rationale: Bounds lock waits only, never statement runtime. Default is 0; the DatabaseSync ctor's {timeout} option sets it. Set to 0 everywhere in the design so that no wait ever happens inside SQLite — busy_timeout=0 is a true non-blocking probe, the pg_try_advisory_lock equivalent. The busy handler is NOT applied to BUSY_SNAPSHOT.

nodes.label: WAL journal mode
nodes.rationale: Readers are never blocked by writers, and a DEFERRED reader pins a snapshot — that is REPEATABLE READ obtained for free, strictly stronger than Postgres READ COMMITTED. Consequence: the explicit repeatable-read isolation option at load/history becomes a no-op, and BEGIN EXCLUSIVE stops blocking readers (it degenerates to IMMEDIATE with a misleading name).

nodes.label: WAL snapshot isolation for readers
nodes.rationale: Measured (exp 09B): a DEFERRED reader saw 2 rows across three writer commits, then 5 after committing. Free repeatable read — but it is exactly why prune's READ-COMMITTED-based C2a argument becomes wrong under WAL.

nodes.label: JS poll-loop lease acquisition
nodes.rationale: busy_timeout=0 + try BEGIN IMMEDIATE + await sleep(pollMs). Load-bearing for two reasons: (a) it keeps the event loop turning so an in-process holder can actually reach its release, and (b) it makes opts.signal genuinely honoured mid-wait (abort at 204 ms against a 200 ms target). Suggested schedule 1 ms for the first 20 ms then 5 ms capped at 25 ms; measured ~1.4 ms overhead per handoff.

nodes.label: L2-B1 — mid-statement cancellation not implementable
nodes.rationale: NOT CLOSEABLE, touches G4 §3. node:sqlite exposes neither sqlite3_interrupt nor a progress handler, and DatabaseSync is synchronous and not structured-cloneable to a Worker. Measured: a 50 ms timer inside a 6033 ms statement never fired. The lease-wait half is recoverable via the poll loop; the long-read half is not, so the contract must narrow from three timings to two and restate 'during a long read' as may still complete.

nodes.label: L2-B2 — no statement_timeout / idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
nodes.rationale: NOT CLOSEABLE, touches G1/G4/G7. SQLite has busy_timeout only, no server and no watchdog thread. TransactionOptions.timeoutMs is a frozen field that becomes validated-then-ignored and faultKind:'timeout' becomes unreachable. This matters MORE under SQLite because an over-running write transaction now blocks every other writer with no server-side backstop.

nodes.label: L2-B3 — withTransaction becomes a whole-database write mutex
nodes.rationale: CLOSEABLE ONLY WITH A SCHEMA/FILE REDESIGN, touches G5. One write lock per database file: a writer to a different table in the same file gets SQLITE_BUSY, and an await inside the callback holds the lock for the whole await (another writer still BUSY 352 ms in). Hard constraint: everything saveAndAdvance touches must live in ONE file, because SQLite does not guarantee atomic commit across ATTACHed databases when any is in WAL mode. Separate files give independent write locks, which is how archive ingest and wallet-sync avoid serialising.
nodes.norm_label: l2-b3 — withtransaction becomes a whole-database write mutex

nodes.label: L2-B4 — SQLite does not poison a transaction after a failed statement
nodes.rationale: CLOSEABLE IN APPLICATION CODE but MANDATORY. Measured: after SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_PRIMARYKEY inside BEGIN IMMEDIATE the next INSERT succeeded and COMMIT committed both surrounding writes. This inverts a documented Postgres safety property: the caller anti-pattern of swallowing an error changes outcome from 'you get nothing' to 'you get a partial transaction'. The adapter must emulate poisoning with a sticky flag on the handle plus forced ROLLBACK — ~20 lines a naive port would not write.
nodes.norm_label: l2-b4 — sqlite does not poison a transaction after a failed statement

nodes.label: L2-B5 — CONNECTION_ERROR has no honest embedded meaning
nodes.rationale: Embedded SQLite has no connection, and the nearest failure modes (CANTOPEN 14, NOTADB 26, CORRUPT 11, READONLY 8, IOERR 10) are all non-retryable. Mapping them onto the retryable CONNECTION_ERROR would be exactly the repurposing STABILITY.md forbids and would make a bounded-retry loop spin on an unopenable file. Recommendation: keep the code (removal is forbidden) and let it become unreachable — the drift test checks table ≡ exported surface, not reachability, so the gate stays green.
nodes.norm_label: l2-b5 — connection_error has no honest embedded meaning

nodes.label: L2-B6 — blocking waits self-deadlock a single-threaded process
nodes.rationale: The naive port (busy_timeout + BEGIN IMMEDIATE) resolves 8 concurrent withLease calls as 1 acquired / 7 LEASE_TIMEOUT in 7018 ms, because the blocking wait pins the single JS thread and the 20 ms holder can never reach the event loop to release. The poll loop makes the identical test 8/8, maxActive 1, 171 ms. Nested withTransaction goes from 'can deadlock under a small pool' to a guaranteed self-deadlock, so SAVEPOINT reentrancy should replace the documented footgun.
nodes.norm_label: l2-b6 — blocking waits self-deadlock a single-threaded process

nodes.label: L2-B7 — filesystem advisory-lock precondition replaces the pooler precondition
nodes.rationale: CLOSEABLE AS DOCUMENTATION. 'No transaction pooler' disappears and is replaced by 'the database and its sidecar lock files must live on a local filesystem with working POSIX advisory locks'. NFS/SMB and WSL's /mnt/c DrvFs are documented-unsafe, and losing lock correctness there silently destroys L1 without erroring — hence a startup probe with the same mandatory-step posture as probeDurability.
nodes.norm_label: l2-b7 — filesystem advisory-lock precondition replaces the pooler precondition

nodes.label: Startup advisory-lock probe
nodes.rationale: Create a throwaway sidecar lock file, take BEGIN IMMEDIATE on it from two in-process connections, assert the second is refused with errcode 5. Turns a silent L1 violation on a broken-lock filesystem into a startup rejection.

nodes.label: SAVEPOINT-based transaction reentrancy
nodes.rationale: SQLite has no nested BEGIN (errcode 1) but SAVEPOINT covers it fully — inner rollback leaves the outer write intact, and a bare SAVEPOINT outside a transaction opens one. Recommended because B6 makes accidental nesting fatal rather than merely risky; it is an additive change (previously-broken code now works), so it is permissible under G2.

nodes.label: In-process write queue
nodes.rationale: Mandatory, not an optimisation: without it two concurrent in-process withTransaction calls on the same connection hit errcode 1 'cannot start a transaction within a transaction'.

nodes.label: SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT (517)
nodes.rationale: A retry-from-scratch error, not a wait error: it returned in 0 ms despite busy_timeout=3000 and does not auto-rollback the reader's transaction. It becomes the SQLite route to TRANSACTION_FAULT(faultKind:'serialization-failure'), replacing Postgres 40001.

nodes.label: SQLITE_LOCKED (6)
nodes.rationale: A same-connection error, not cross-process: DDL while a cursor is open on that table. Directly relevant to the migration runner, which must use a dedicated connection and materialise every result set before running DDL.

nodes.label: Throwing UDF as a cooperative interrupt
nodes.rationale: The only cooperative interrupt available: a throwing user-defined function aborts a running statement (threw at 301 ms out of a ~6 s query). Disclosed with its limits — it requires injecting a check function into the query text, works only where the planner re-invokes it per row, and cannot help a BEGIN IMMEDIATE lock wait or an index-only scan. A targeted mitigation for chain-archive scans, not a general answer.
nodes.norm_label: throwing udf as a cooperative interrupt

nodes.label: Kernel crash-release of the fcntl lock on SIGKILL
nodes.rationale: Measured: after SIGKILL of a holder inside an open BEGIN IMMEDIATE, the successor acquired the write lock in 0 ms, the uncommitted row was gone, integrity_check was ok, and the -wal/-shm files were reclaimed. This is the property the whole lease design rests on.
nodes.norm_label: kernel crash-release of the fcntl lock on sigkill

nodes.label: Rejected: lock-table row + heartbeat + stale takeover
nodes.rationale: Rejected on the project's own prior grounds. Without a heartbeat it deadlocks forever; with one, safety rests on 'no live holder is ever stalled longer than T', which is unknowable — a GC pause, a swapping host, a paused debugger or a frozen WSL VM resumes and writes after being declared dead. This is exactly the TTL/lease-stealing design STORAGE_ALGEBRA already removed, and choosing it would silently reopen a closed decision and downgrade L1 from unconditional to conditional on a liveness assumption.
nodes.norm_label: rejected: lock-table row + heartbeat + stale takeover

nodes.label: Rejected: BEGIN EXCLUSIVE held open on the main DB
nodes.rationale: Correct on crash-release but rejected on granularity: it is whole-database, so it cannot express per-key leases like wallet-sync:{networkId} and it serialises writers holding no lease at all. Also measured: in WAL mode EXCLUSIVE does not even block readers — it is IMMEDIATE with a misleading name.
nodes.norm_label: rejected: begin exclusive held open on the main db

nodes.label: flock(2) and fcntl POSIX record locks are independent lock spaces
nodes.rationale: Measured: SQLite wrote successfully while an external flock -x held the same file. So flock is safe as a separate lease channel but useless as a fence against SQLite writers, and anyone assuming otherwise gets a silent mutual-exclusion hole. Node core exposes no flock/fcntl binding anyway, so that route needs a native addon the sidecar design avoids.
nodes.norm_label: flock(2) and fcntl posix record locks are independent lock spaces

nodes.label: prune under BEGIN IMMEDIATE and the C2a re-derivation
nodes.rationale: prune's grace-window TOCTOU argument explicitly depends on READ COMMITTED per-row re-evaluation. Under WAL a DEFERRED prune evaluates NOT EXISTS against a snapshot, so a chunk re-referenced by a later-committing save still looks unreferenced — a direct C2a violation. Under IMMEDIATE no other writer can commit for the transaction's duration, so C2a becomes trivially true and actually gets stronger, but the justifying sentence in the code and STORAGE_ALGEBRA §2 is wrong as written and must be re-derived, not copy-pasted. The 15-minute grace window stops being load-bearing for safety.
nodes.norm_label: prune under begin immediate and the c2a re-derivation

nodes.label: P10 lease mutual-exclusion property test
nodes.rationale: 8 concurrent withLease calls on one key with a 20 ms critical section and instrumented maxActive. Passes only with the poll-loop design and fails 7/8 with the naive port. The sidecar design makes a genuine multi-process P10 cheap and meaningful for the first time.

nodes.label: G5 — co-transactionality
nodes.rationale: 'Both durable at one commit or neither.' Survives under SQLite only if everything saveAndAdvance touches lives in one database file, because cross-ATTACH commit atomicity is not guaranteed in WAL mode.

nodes.label: G7 — timeouts
nodes.rationale: statementTimeoutMs / idleInTxTimeoutMs have no SQLite implementation; DEFAULT_* constants stay exported but stop meaning anything. A real capability loss, worsened by B3's whole-file write mutex.

nodes.label: Single-writer-process promise vs in-process mutual exclusion
nodes.rationale: CONTRACT.md says do not run two writer processes, and P10's guarantee is connection-scoped, so the obligation that must actually hold is mutual exclusion between concurrent async callers and connections inside one process. A pure in-process JS mutex (~30 lines) would satisfy the letter of the promise but is recommended against: it silently discards crash release and protection against an accidental second process (a stray CLI, a leftover supervisor, a --watch reload overlapping the old process).
nodes.norm_label: single-writer-process promise vs in-process mutual exclusion

nodes.label: node:sqlite (recommended driver)
nodes.rationale: RECOMMENDED. The only candidate that takes UmbraDB's runtime dependency graph from {postgres, zod} to {zod}: zero new packages, zero native binaries, nothing for npm audit --omit=dev or the ignore-scripts=true supply-chain gate, and nothing that can fail the packed-tarball smoke test on an unsupported platform. Ships the newest SQLite of any candidate (3.53.1) and exposes UDFs, aggregates, an async backup(), VACUUM INTO, sessions/changesets and extension loading.

nodes.label: DatabaseSync
nodes.rationale: Synchronous handle; not structured-cloneable to a Worker. Accepts { readOnly, enableForeignKeyConstraints, allowExtension, timeout, readBigInts, returnArrays }, and silently ignores unknown options — so forwarding today's Postgres option bag would appear to work while dropping every durability bound.

nodes.label: better-sqlite3 (candidate)
nodes.rationale: Not rejected on install failure — the native-addon supply-chain hypothesis was REFUTED by measurement: v13 declares no install/postinstall script, ships 8 prebuilds in the tarball, and installed clean under ignore-scripts=true. The case against it rests on 27 MB, two extra packages, an N-API binary in a package whose supply-chain workflow exists to keep foreign code out, and the tail risk of a platform with no prebuild.

nodes.label: @libsql/client (candidate)
nodes.rationale: Async and has an in-driver interrupt, but adds 15 runtime packages / 23 MB and ships a FORKED SQLite 3.45.1 — the oldest engine of any candidate. Blobs come back as ArrayBuffer rather than Buffer.

nodes.label: bun:sqlite (candidate)
nodes.rationale: DISQUALIFIED ON PACKAGING, NOT CAPABILITY. UmbraDB is a library published to npm declaring engines node >=24 with a strict exports map, and pack-smoke.yml / supply-chain.yml / conformance.yml all run setup-node 24. Adopting it would make the package runtime-exclusive to Bun and break every Node consumer plus all three CI gates. The earlier 'Bun is not viable here' finding was about bun + mongodb and does not apply — bun:sqlite itself works fine on this machine.

nodes.label: postgres.js-shaped tagged-template shim
nodes.rationale: SHIM, NOT REWRITE. A ~250-line src/sqlite/sql.ts reimplementing sql``, sql(ident), sql.json, sql.array, sql.unsafe, sql.reserve, sql.begin with SAVEPOINT nesting, query.cancel() and query.cursor(n). A 130-line prototype ran real PgTemporalKV queries verbatim with the only edits being schema-qualification and dropped ::casts. Decisive argument: a native-API rewrite would be 3-4x larger and would hit the Date-to-NULL, boolean and readBigInts traps once per call site instead of once per codebase — with the Date trap failing silently in exactly the code path implementing the Lean-mechanized law T3. Overhead measured at 1.59x over raw prepared statements (5.23 µs vs 3.28 µs), noise against a networked Postgres round trip.

nodes.label: columns() declared-type-name row decoding
nodes.rationale: THE DECISIVE DISCOVERY. StatementSync.columns() returns each result column's declared type name verbatim (JSONB, TIMESTAMPTZ, BYTEA, BIGINT, INT4) because SQLite stores declared type text verbatim even though affinity ignores it, and SQLITE_ENABLE_COLUMN_METADATA is compiled into Node's build. That lets the shim key a decoder table off declared type names exactly as postgres.js keys off type OIDs, with zero annotation at any of the 190 call sites. Verified full row-shape parity: value as parsed object, version as bigint, written_at as a real Date, size_bytes as number, hash as Buffer, count(*) as bigint. This is what makes the shim not a semantic-difference-hider: the type boundary is closed structurally in one table.

nodes.label: STRICT tables vs the declared-type decoder
nodes.rationale: Unsettled trade-off: STRICT tables accept only INT/INTEGER/REAL/TEXT/BLOB/ANY as declared types, so STRICT and the Postgres-name decoder convention are mutually exclusive. Column-name-keyed decoding is the escape hatch if STRICT wins.
nodes.norm_label: strict tables vs the declared-type decoder

nodes.label: Dedicated writer worker thread topology
nodes.rationale: One worker owns the single DatabaseSync; the main thread talks to it over postMessage plus a SharedArrayBuffer cancel flag. Justified because it is the ONLY way to restore mid-query cancellation and to stop synchronous work stalling a wallet client's event loop: measured cancellation latency ~1 ms with max main-loop lag 0.6 ms, versus a 103 ms scan completing with signal.aborted still false in-process. Costs 32x per-operation latency (3.86 µs to 124 µs), which is still ~8k ops/s. UmbraDB is already single-writer so it costs nothing architecturally.

nodes.label: SharedArrayBuffer cancel flag
nodes.rationale: An Int32Array the main thread sets and the worker's UDF polls with Atomics.load — the cross-thread channel that makes query.cancel() real again. Measured: an 8M-row scan cancelled 1 ms after the flag was set.

nodes.label: umbradb_guard() deadline/cancel UDF
nodes.rationale: One mechanism for both cancellation and statement_timeout: appended as AND umbradb_guard() = 0 to every long-running statement, amortising checks to every 256th row at ~68 ns/row. Measured: a 50 ms deadline honoured at 51 ms, SAB cancel honoured at +1 ms. Statements where appending it is impossible run uncancellable and must be documented.

nodes.label: L3-B1 — mid-query AbortSignal cancellation impossible on a synchronous main-thread driver
nodes.rationale: node:sqlite exposes no sqlite3_interrupt and no progress handler, and on the main thread there is nobody to call it — the loop is blocked. Proved directly: a 103 ms scan completed with signal.aborted false even though abort() had been scheduled at t+20 ms. Closeable ONLY by moving the database into a worker thread, or by demoting the G4 contract from abortable to deadline-bounded.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b1 — mid-query abortsignal cancellation impossible on a synchronous main-thread driver

nodes.label: L3-B2 — a synchronous driver blocks the event loop proportionally to the work
nodes.rationale: Measured against a 0.15-0.3 ms idle baseline: a LIKE count(*) scan blocks 34 ms, .all() of 500k rows blocks 430 ms, a 64 MiB BLOB write 237 ms and read 162 ms. This matters because UmbraDB is embedded in a Midnight wallet whose sync loop, RPC keep-alives and UI share that loop — a 430 ms stall is a dropped websocket heartbeat. Partially closeable: iterate() chunked at 256 rows costs worst-case 2.9 ms per batch, the shape listKeys already has; big single blobs cannot be chunked without incremental BLOB I/O that node:sqlite does not expose.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b2 — a synchronous driver blocks the event loop proportionally to the work

nodes.label: L3-B3 — UmbraDBSql is a frozen public type and cannot survive
nodes.rationale: NOT CLOSEABLE. UmbraDBSql is structurally the postgres.js Sql type, re-exported from the barrel and taken by every adapter constructor. Even a perfectly shaped shim is not the same nominal type, and dropping the postgres dependency removes the type's declaration entirely. Breaks G1 and G2 — this is a 2.0.0.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b3 — umbradbsql is a frozen public type and cannot survive

nodes.label: L3-B4 — createClient's option surface is Postgres-shaped end to end
nodes.rationale: connectionString, maxConnections, connectTimeout, statementTimeoutMs, lockTimeoutMs, idleInTxTimeoutMs are all meaningless for an embedded engine, as are assertNoConflictingSearchPath and the 63-byte identifier bound. maxConnections in particular has no meaning: there is one writer, enforced by SQLite. Closeable with a redesign, but it is a G1/G2 break.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b4 — createclient's option surface is postgres-shaped end to end

nodes.label: L3-B5 — SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER is 32,766 but UmbraDB batches bind 60,000
nodes.rationale: CHUNK_INSERT_MAX_ROWS=30,000 (2 params/row) and JUNCTION_INSERT_MAX_ROWS=20,000 (3 params/row) were sized against Postgres's 65,534 cap. Measured thresholds: 16,383x2 prepares, 16,384x2 fails; 10,922x3 prepares, 10,923x3 fails. Closeable by retuning to 16,000/10,000, but that doubles the statement count per save — which changes the 'EXACTLY ONE statement per checkpoint' property those comments defend — and it is a silent runtime failure if missed.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b5 — sqlite_max_variable_number is 32,766 but umbradb batches bind 60,000

nodes.label: L3-B6 — a Date bound positionally is silently stored as NULL
nodes.rationale: node:sqlite treats a non-Uint8Array object argument as a named-parameter bag; a Date has no own enumerable keys so parameter 1 is never bound — no error. Arrays and class instances throw; the Date case is the one that fails silently. It bites at getAtImpl's ${asOf.at}::timestamptz, i.e. the point-in-time read that IS T3, so a naive port returns the wrong row with no error and no test failure. Closed once in the driver layer by normalize() converting Date to ISO-8601 text — the strongest single argument for the shim over a rewrite.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b6 — a date bound positionally is silently stored as null

nodes.label: L3-B7 — booleans are rejected outright
nodes.rationale: run(true) throws 'Provided value cannot be bound to SQLite parameter 1'. Bites at chain-archive-store's isCanonical/finalized binds. Closeable in the driver layer (normalize maps true->1/false->0) and loud, so cheap to find even without the shim.

nodes.label: L3-B8 — sql.array() + GIN <@ containment has no driver-level equivalent
nodes.rationale: SQLite has no array type and no GIN. The shim can only serialize an array to a JSON text parameter for json_each(); whether that is an acceptable index strategy is L4/L1's call. Driver-level fact: 6 sql.array sites total.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b8 — sql.array() + gin <@ containment has no driver-level equivalent

nodes.label: L3-B9 — text PostgreSQL rejects, SQLite silently mangles
nodes.rationale: A NUL byte in TEXT is accepted but length() reports 1 for 'a\0b' while the JS round trip returns three code units, so LIKE/length()/ordering disagree with the stored value. A lone surrogate is accepted and silently replaced with U+FFFD. Already closed by hasPostgresUnsafeText — but under SQLite that guard stops meaning 'PostgreSQL cannot store either' and starts meaning 'SQLite corrupts either'. Any migration cleanup that relaxes it as Postgres-specific would introduce silent data corruption: rename it, do not delete it.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b9 — text postgresql rejects, sqlite silently mangles

nodes.label: L3-B10 — readBigInts is per-statement/per-database, never per-column
nodes.rationale: Default number mode THROWS ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE outside the safe range rather than losing precision silently, with exactly one hole: INT64_MIN comes back as a number with no throw (exact, since it is -2^63, so a type-discipline hole not precision loss; unreachable in practice because version/height/id are non-negative — record it, don't fix it). With setReadBigInts(true) every integer column becomes bigint, including int4 columns postgres.js returns as number. Closed in the driver layer: read everything as bigint, then downcast columns whose declared type is INT4/INTEGER/SMALLINT.
nodes.norm_label: l3-b10 — readbigints is per-statement/per-database, never per-column

nodes.rationale: Measured compile option; flagged to L4 because an ATTACH-per-schema design has a hard ceiling of 10 attached databases.

nodes.label: SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH = 1 GB
nodes.rationale: Caps any single BLOB/TEXT; flagged to L5 for the chain archive.

nodes.label: normalize() bind normalisation
nodes.rationale: Non-negotiable: undefined|null -> null, boolean -> 0|1, Date -> ISO-8601 text, Buffer -> Uint8Array, everything else passthrough, and THROW on any other object rather than let it become a named-parameter bag. Closes B6 and B7 in one place.

nodes.label: db.createTagStore()
nodes.rationale: Node 24's built-in tagged-template façade with automatic statement caching, measured identical to hand-prepared statements and injection-safe. A good fallback but not sufficient alone: no identifier interpolation, no promise interface, no row decoding.

nodes.label: hasPostgresUnsafeText guard
nodes.rationale: Rejects NUL bytes and lone surrogates. Must survive the migration under a new name; deleting it as 'Postgres-specific' would introduce silent SQLite data corruption.

nodes.label: backup() and VACUUM INTO
nodes.rationale: backup(src, dest, {rate, progress}) returns a real Promise and VACUUM INTO produced a readable copy — both directly serve G4's backup/restore contract and are strictly better than the Postgres adapter, which has no in-library backup at all.

nodes.label: ignore-scripts=true supply-chain gate
nodes.rationale: Asserted by supply-chain.yml against the repo-root .npmrc. The hypothesis that it would break better-sqlite3 was refuted by measurement; what would have had to be true is a prebuild-install postinstall step, which older versions had.

nodes.label: iterate() chunked reads with a macrotask tick per batch
nodes.rationale: 256-row batches cost worst-case 2.9 ms each (258 ms total for 500k rows); awaiting a macrotask tick between batches keeps the loop responsive, and it is exactly the shape listKeys already has.
nodes.norm_label: iterate() chunked reads with a macrotask tick per batch

nodes.label: The sync/async fault line: microtask ordering preserved, macrotask liveness destroyed
nodes.rationale: Not the blocker it looks like. Awaiting an already-resolved value still drains the microtask queue, so the relative interleaving of concurrent UmbraDB callers is bit-identical to today (A0 B0 A1 B1 A2 B2 under both real I/O and resolved values). What a synchronous driver destroys is macrotask liveness: 100,000 resolved-value awaits ran to completion in 9 ms with a setTimeout(…,0) still un-fired. The one fatal consequence is that an AbortSignal can never fire while a synchronous query runs on the same thread.
nodes.norm_label: the sync/async fault line: microtask ordering preserved, macrotask liveness destroyed

nodes.label: Recorded false negative: the 0.0 ms event-loop lag artefact
nodes.rationale: A separate measurement reported 'max event-loop lag 0.0 ms' for the same .all(); that number is an artefact because the setInterval probe was installed and cleared without ever getting a tick — the synchronous work ran to completion before the first timer could fire. Recorded explicitly because it is exactly the shape of a false negative the brief warns about.
nodes.norm_label: recorded false negative: the 0.0 ms event-loop lag artefact

nodes.label: Open question: node:sqlite's documented stability index
nodes.rationale: Verified empirically that it needs no flag, emits no ExperimentalWarning and reports process.versions.sqlite, but the docs' stability marker could not be checked offline. If it is still Release Candidate the API could change within Node 24's lifetime, and createTagStore, backup, columns()'s type field and setReadBigInts are all things the design leans on. The single largest unquantified risk in the lane.
